Dec 04, 2025: Vesta Announces Three New Lease Agreements Totaling More Than 550 Thousand Square Feet

Corporacion Inmobiliaria Vesta, S.A.B. de C.V. ("Vesta") (NYSE: VTMX; BMV: VESTA), a fully-integrated, internally managed real estate company that owns, manages, develops and leases industrial properties in Mexico, announced that it has entered into three new lease agreements for a total of more than 550 thousand square feet, underscoring continued progress on the Company's Route 2030 strategic growth plan.

"We are very pleased to see companies' continued confidence in Mexico through long-term investments that strengthen and consolidate the industrial real estate market. The sustained demand we're seeing drives a stronger and more resilient platform for growth while fostering employment and development across our communities," said Mario Chacon, Vesta's Chief Commercial Officer.

At Vesta Park Mega Region, Tijuana's most connected and scalable industrial park, Vesta leased two buildings totaling 473,601 square feet to a tenant in the electronics sector, deepening Vesta's diversification within this industry. Further, with these two new agreements, Vesta Park Mega Region is now fully leased and stabilized.

In Queretaro, Vesta executed a lease for a 81,600 square feet build-to-suit facility with an internationally recognized aerospace company, acknowledged as one of the leading players in its industry.

Both the Tijuana and Queretaro markets continue to reflect robust fundamentals, supported by solid infrastructure and an abundant, highly qualified labor force. This underscores Mexico's appeal for companies seeking cost-competitive production and logistics advantages, reflected in their confidence in investing in Mexico and in partnering with Vesta.

(OMA), a leading airport operator in Mexico, manages a network of 13 airports primarily in the northern and central regions, including key hubs like Monterrey. Its core business revolves around aeronautical services, such as passenger and cargo handling, alongside non-aeronautical activities including retail concessions, real estate development, and commercial leasing. OMA's fastest-growing segments include international passenger traffic, driven by increasing tourism and trade links, as well as cargo operations, which have expanded with e-commerce and cross-border logistics. Additionally, the company has seen robust growth in non-aeronautical revenues from diversified sources like parking and advertising, supporting overall profitability. Through strategic investments in infrastructure and technology, OMA enhances operational efficiency and passenger experience, positioning itself as a vital player in Mexico's aviation sector. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 11th largest Airlines company by market capitalization.

In 2026, Mexico raised the IEPS on sugar-sweetened beverages by nearly 87%, to MX$3.08 per liter, and in response Coca-Cola FEMSA prioritized affordable pricing and large multi-serve formats in traditional retail. Mexico sales volume grew 4.2% in the third quarter, but the operating margin for Mexico and Central America fell 170 basis points to 14.3% as rising freight costs compounded a weaker price mix. Water volumes grew 20.2%, five times faster than soft drinks, pointing to a structural shift in consumer demand that bottlers, retailers and beverage manufacturers will need to address.

Higher beverage taxes and tighter household budgets weighed on consumption in Mexico during the third quarter, while markets such as Colombia and Brazil gained ground in regional performance. As consumer habits shift, alternatives to soft drinks are becoming increasingly popular among Mexicans.

According to The Coca-Cola Company's quarterly financial report, the company faced a consumer environment in Mexico pressured by the tax increase on flavored beverages with added sugars. As part of the 2026 Economic Package, the Special Tax on Production and Services (IEPS) on these beverages rose from MX$1.6/L in 2025 to M$X3.08/L (US$0.086/L - US$0.16/L) starting in January, an increase of nearly 87%. Beverages with non-caloric sweeteners, such as light or zero versions, were also taxed, at a rate of MX$1.5/L.

The adjustment reached store shelves in December 2025, when soft drink prices rose by up to 20%. In the first half of January, soft drink inflation reached 3.9%, the largest increase for a comparable period since 2014. "In Mexico, the environment remains challenging, but we are seeing encouraging progress," said Henrique Braun, CEO, The Coca-Cola Company, during the earnings call with investors. He attributed this progress to affordability strategies, revenue growth management and locally relevant marketing.

Affordability Over Margins

The tax increase coincided with greater price sensitivity among Mexican households, which shifted their purchases toward neighborhood grocery stores in search of presentations that offered better value for money. One example is the 3L bottle, whose sales grew more than Coca-Cola FEMSA had budgeted. Coca-Cola FEMSA is the largest franchise bottler of Coca-Cola products in the world by sales volume.

Executives explained that this behavior reflects a decision made at the start of the year: in response to the IEPS increase, the company prioritized affordable prices to avoid losing scale, especially in traditional retail. "This year, and this is by design, we decided to maintain our competitive position and our scale, especially in traditional trade, favoring affordability," said Gerardo Cruz, CFO, Coca-Cola FEMSA.

In terms of volume, the bet paid off. Sales in Mexico grew 4.2% in unit cases during the quarter, and Coca-Cola FEMSA gained 70 basis points of value share in soft drinks as of September. Cruz acknowledged that volume in Mexico comfortably exceeded the budget and that much of the surprise came from multi-serve presentations. Larger bottles offer a better price per liter and keep sales going, but their growing share of the sales mix erodes average pricing.

The results for Mexico and Central America illustrate this trade-off. Revenue rose 8.3% and gross profit 11.6%, but operating income fell 3.1% and the operating margin contracted 170 basis points to 14.3%. In a quarter of record consolidated volume, the region was one of the main sources of pressure.

Logistics explain most of the decline in profit margins. Higher volume forced the company to ship large amounts of product from its Toluca plant to the southeast, which raised transportation costs. In response, the company has proposed a long-term project to build a new plant in southeastern Mexico to cut the transportation costs that have climbed as sales volume in the region has grown.

"Our freight expenses have increased significantly compared to last year. This is something we are obviously looking to address, by focusing on efficiencies at our existing plants in the southeast and a long-term project for a new plant in that region," said Cruz.

Water Grows Five Times Faster Than Soda

Consumers also showed a stronger preference for water over carbonated soft drinks, with water growing five times faster. Between July and September 2026, the volume of water sold in Coca-Cola FEMSA's Mexican operations rose about 20.2%, while soft drinks advanced 3.9%, compared with the same period of 2025.

Soft drinks still hold a wide lead in volume sold, but the surprise lies in how fast water is growing. According to the quarterly report, the water category includes flavored options and excludes presentations larger than 5L. Jugs are counted separately and grew only 0.5%.

Against this backdrop, Ian Craig, CEO, Coca-Cola FEMSA, highlighted the performance of new products. During the quarter, the company launched Coca-Cola Triple Zero, as well as Topo Chico Sparkling Lemonade and Orangeade. The two Topo Chico drinks reached 70% coverage in traditional retail and a 40% repurchase rate. In addition, Ciel Aguas Frescas, launched the previous quarter, reached 65% coverage in traditional retail and has gained 7.6 percentage points of market share since its launch in May.

Craig noted that Coca-Cola maintains a solid commercial performance and that its innovations are being well received. He explained that the company's priority is to keep growing volume, gain market share and develop new beverage categories, while gradually improving profitability through disciplined spending and operational efficiencies. "We have to be mindful that the consumer environment remains difficult, but anything we see now will be practically industry-wide," he said.

Mexico Lags as South America Accelerates

During the presentation of quarterly results, Braun said Mexico has become the most challenging market for driving sales. "While growth remains strong in other countries in the region, in Mexico it will take a bit more time to regain momentum," he noted.

Outside Mexico and Central America, South America posted a 14.7% increase in revenue, with Brazil and Colombia among the markets that drove regional performance during the same period. Brazil remained strong, with volume growth across several categories and market share gains. In Colombia, the company also reported solid progress, although management noted that demand was creating supply constraints. Guatemala and Argentina contributed to regional results to a lesser extent.

"South America delivered a solid performance, driven by double-digit operating income growth in Brazil and Colombia. The acceleration of our digital transformation and the dynamism of our broad portfolio further strengthened our leadership position," said Craig.

A Playbook Tested in 2014

According to Bloomberg Línea, the company is preparing a course correction for Mexico together with its bottlers Coca-Cola FEMSA and Arca Continental. The goal is to withstand the new IEPS levy and adapt its commercial strategy starting this year. "We will all be hands-on to implement the latest adaptations of the strategy now that we know the final policy," said James Quincey, Chairman and CEO, The Coca-Cola Company.

Quincey recalled that Coca-Cola faced a similar tax in 2014 and managed to adapt through marketing, innovation and revenue growth management (RGM), a tool that adjusts prices and promotions to protect profitability.

Bottom line: Consumer Sentiment fell to 51.7 in August 2026, down 11% year-over-year - with little bearing on a copper producer whose realizations are set in global markets. Q2 2026 net income rose 71.6% to a record $1,670.0 million and net sales 40.6% to $4,289.0 million, even as mined copper production fell 3.5%: price, not volume, delivered the entire result.

Commodity producers sell into global markets, so a U.S. household survey is at best a partial input into the demand picture. The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index measures how American families view their own finances and the economy over the next one and five years, and because consumer spending drives an estimated two-thirds to 70% of U.S. GDP, it reads well on domestic retail demand - but copper is priced on the London Metal Exchange and COMEX, where the marginal buyer is more likely to be a Chinese construction or grid project. The final August 2026 reading came in at 51.7, revised up from a preliminary 51.0 but still 6% below July's 55.2 and 11% below the year-ago level, leaving the index below the 1st percentile of its recorded history. Expectations drove the decline rather than current conditions: the one-year outlook fell 10% and the five-year outlook fell 13%, on inflation concerns (one-year inflation expectations of 4.0%, five-year expectations of 3.3%) and Iran-related gas-price fears. This report was generated off the August final reading, never off a preliminary number. A preliminary September reading arrives September 11, 2026; this report will be regenerated once that reading is finalized.

SectorCopper Mining / Diversified Metals
Impact TypeMinimal, Indirect - the least clean mechanism in coverage, and potentially misleading: record profitability coincided with a near-record-low sentiment reading
Index Reading51.7 (Aug 2026, final)
MechanismU.S. household confidence is a marginal input into global copper demand, which is dominated by Chinese consumption, grid electrification, and data-center construction; realized prices are set on international exchanges
Quantified ExposureEffectively none that can be isolated. The cleanest evidence is the quarter itself: net income rose 71.6% and sales 40.6% while mined copper production fell 3.5% and every by-product declined - price, not volume, drove the result
Q2 2026 net sales$4,289.0M, +40.6% YoY - a record; first-half sales of $8,540.4M vs. $6,172.9M
Q2 2026 net income / EPS$1,670.0M, +71.6% from $973.4M - a record; income per share $2.01 vs. $1.17; net income margin 38.9% vs. 31.9%
Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA$2,856.0M at a 66.6% margin; first-half adjusted EBITDA of $5,570.0M, +57.5%
Mined copper production230,662 tonnes, -3.5% - a 12% decline at Peruvian mines outweighing a 3.2% increase in Mexico; FY26 guidance of 917,000 tons
By-product productionSilver -3.8%, zinc -14.5%, molybdenum -11.0%
Operating cash cost per pound$(0.03) for the first six months of 2026, net of by-product revenue credits - negative, meaning by-products more than covered cash costs
Capital deploymentCapital investment $422.8M, +79.4%; $1,250.0M of ten-year senior unsecured notes issued June 24, 2026 at 5.350%; Q3 2026 declared dividend value of approximately $3.23/share

Source: Southern Copper Corporation second-quarter and six-months 2026 results release filed July 21, 2026, and earnings call, July 22, 2026.

Impact on Southern Copper Corporation (NYSE:SCCO)

The chain connecting a U.S. sentiment survey to Southern Copper's income statement is long and weak. Copper is priced on international exchanges, where the marginal buyer is far more likely to be a Chinese construction or grid project than an American household. Southern Copper's own second quarter is the cleanest available demonstration: net income rose 71.6% to a record $1,670.0 million and net sales rose 40.6% to $4,289.0 million while the company actually mined 3.5% less copper and produced less silver, zinc, and molybdenum than a year earlier. Price, not volume, delivered the entire result. If U.S. consumer demand were a meaningful driver, a sentiment reading below the 1st percentile of its history would not coincide with record copper realizations.

For the second quarter of fiscal 2026 (filed July 21, 2026), adjusted EBITDA reached $2,856.0 million at a 66.6% margin, and operating cash cost per pound of copper net of by-product credits was $(0.03) for the first half - negative, meaning by-product revenue more than covered cash costs. Raul Jacob, Vice President of Finance, Treasurer and CFO, told investors on the July 22, 2026 call that the company posted "record-breaking results in sales, adjusted EBITDA, and net income," attributing them to operating excellence amid sustained demand for copper and its by-products. Management expects sales volumes to improve in the second half as first-half material becomes available for sale, and set full-year copper production guidance at 917,000 tons.

Forward catalyst: Southern Copper is expected to report third-quarter 2026 results on or around October 26, 2026, per analyst consensus scheduling. Two company-specific items carry more weight than any macro print. First, leadership: Leonardo Contreras Lerdo de Tejada was appointed interim chief executive effective April 16, 2026 and confirmed on April 23, succeeding a chief executive of more than two decades, making the second quarter his second reporting period. Second, project execution in Peru, where the Tia Maria project and permitting progress remain exposed to regulatory and community friction, funded in part by the $1,250.0 million note issuance completed in June 2026. The University of Michigan's preliminary September Consumer Sentiment reading (due September 11, 2026) is not a factor for this name.

Analyst snapshot: As of the most recent available data, 18 analysts polled by S&P Global Market Intelligence rated Southern Copper a consensus "Sell," with an average 12-month price target of $168.15 and a range of $128.50 to $250 - roughly 6% below the $179.29 closing price on July 24, 2026. A 17-analyst tally updated September 3, 2026 showed a comparable average target of $169.06 and an unchanged "Sell" consensus, with valuation relative to the recent share-price move cited as the principal concern. The Governing Board of the Central Bank of Chile (BCCh) has maintained interest rates at 4.5% for the seventh consecutive meeting, though it will remain vigilant for any signs of greater transmission or persistence of inflation due to shocks and heightened uncertainty, which is "greater than usual."

"The risks for inflation have significantly increased. While overall CPI data has been in line with expectations, projections for the coming months have risen markedly, placing them above the trajectory of the central scenario of the Monetary Policy Report (IPoM)," it explained in a statement.

"This occurs in a context where near-term prospects for activity are being downgraded, mainly due to supply factors linked to mining and the climatic shock. While it is anticipated that the local economy will regain momentum toward 2027, it cannot be ruled out that its current weakness may persist longer than expected," it added.

The BCCh has noted that the "unusual intensity" of the El Niño phenomenon has already begun to weigh on international food prices, alongside rising costs for energy, transportation, and fertilizers due to the war in Iran. However, copper prices remained close to the levels recorded at the previous meeting.

Additionally, the central bank has observed a tightening of international financial conditions in an environment characterized by expectations of a more restrictive monetary policy stance, falling stock markets, a strengthening U.S. dollar, and rising long-term interest rates.

The reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil opens a new landscape for business between Chile and the largest economy in Latin America. Infrastructure, energy, and mining are among the sectors that could provide opportunities for Chilean companies over the next four years, alongside the continuity of the president's agenda for reindustrialization and energy transition.

This was stated by the president of the Chilean-Brazilian Chamber of Commerce, Selma Nunes, who emphasized that the Nova Indústria Brasil program, driven by the government, offers opportunities for Chilean companies involved in renewable energies, sustainable mining, infrastructure, and technological services.

"The greatest opportunities for Chilean companies lie not only in traditional trade but in the integration into value chains and the transfer of technological innovation," she stated.

YOU MAY BE INTERESTED

Among the initiatives that could open business opportunities, Nunes highlighted the development of the Bioceanic Corridor and concession programs in Brazil, which would allow Chilean firms in engineering, port services, concession management, construction, and international transport to integrate into regional logistics chains.

In the energy sector, she pointed to the complementarity between Chile's renewable generation capacity and Brazil's industrial demand, particularly in the development of green hydrogen to decarbonize steel production and fertilization. There are also opportunities in electromobility, through the integration of Chilean lithium and refined copper with Brazil's metalworking and automotive industries to manufacture batteries, heavy components, and electric vehicles.

The leader also identified areas for cooperation in data centers, agribusiness, and financial technology.

Regarding the expansion and acquisition plans of Chilean companies in Brazil, Nunes stated that the continuity of the president allows for greater predictability regarding industrial and regulatory policies.

"We do not see a slowdown, but rather a differentiated assessment by type of business," she noted. In her view, companies that were considering entering or expanding in Brazil would maintain those plans, given the continued attractiveness of the Brazilian market.

The Z-score formula for predicting bankruptcy was first published in 1968 by Professor Altman (Professor of Finance at New York University). The formula uses accounting ratios to predict whether a company could go bankrupt within two years with some studies showing it has an 80% accuracy rate for certain sectors. Some investors rely on it as a guide in assessing a company's financial strength and a way to mitigate risk, whereas others prefer different models that rely on market-based data instead. The score can also be useful to determine whether a company is heading in a positive or negative direction even though it may have zero risk of actual bankruptcy.

There are three variations of the Z-score and we have measured Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste de with all three variations.

A Z score above >2.99 is considered "safe", a score between 1.81 and 2.99 is considered "grey" and a Z score under 1.81 is considered "distressed".

The Beneish model is a statistical model that uses financial ratios to determine whether it is possible that a company's earnings may have been embellished or window dressed. Because it is a probability model it is used as one of several tools by investors to mitigate risk.

5.1 Activities

Arca Continental SAB de CV, a prominent Mexican conglomerate, is primarily engaged in the production, bottling, and distribution of beverages as a key franchise partner for The Coca-Cola Company. The company operates across Mexico, the United States, and South America, offering a diverse portfolio that includes carbonated soft drinks, bottled water, juices, teas, and snacks. Its core activities encompass manufacturing, logistics, and sales through an extensive network of distribution channels, serving both retail and hospitality sectors. In recent years, the fastest-growing segments have been healthier beverage options, such as flavored waters and ready-to-drink teas, driven by shifting consumer preferences toward wellness and hydration products. Additionally, international expansion into markets like Ecuador and Peru has fueled growth, enhancing revenue streams and market share. Arca Continental's strategic investments in sustainability and digital technologies further support its operational efficiency and long-term competitiveness in the global beverage industry. It is Mexico's largest Beverages company by market capitalization.

5.1 Activities

Promotora Y Operadora De Infraestructura, S.A.B. De C.V. (PINFRA), a leading Mexican infrastructure company listed on the Mexican Stock Exchange, specializes in the development, construction, operation, and maintenance of transportation and infrastructure assets. Its core activities encompass toll roads, bridges, airports, and railways, primarily through public-private concessions that generate revenue via user fees and long-term contracts. The company plays a vital role in Mexico's economic growth by enhancing connectivity and mobility across key regions. Among its fastest-growing segments are airport operations, which have expanded significantly due to increasing passenger traffic and new terminal developments, as well as concessions for modern toll highways that benefit from rising vehicular demand and government infrastructure initiatives. PINFRA's strategic focus on sustainable projects and operational efficiency has positioned it as a key player in the sector, contributing to national development while delivering consistent returns for shareholders. It is Mexico's 3rd largest Engineering & construction company by market capitalization.

SECTION 6 CORPORATE PROFILE

6.1 Activities

Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. (PINFRA), is a leading Mexican company specializing in the development, operation, and maintenance of infrastructure assets. Its core business activities encompass the management of toll road concessions, airport operations, and railway systems, primarily in Mexico, with a focus on enhancing connectivity and efficiency in transportation networks. The company has diversified into complementary areas such as industrial and urban infrastructure projects, leveraging public-private partnerships to drive growth. Among its fastest-growing segments are toll road concessions, fueled by increasing vehicular traffic and strategic expansions, as well as airport operations, which have benefited from rising passenger volumes and modernization efforts. PINFRA's commitment to sustainable practices and operational excellence positions it as a key player in Mexico's infrastructure sector, supporting economic development through reliable and innovative solutions. It is the International Depository Receipt (IDR) market's 11th largest Engineering & construction company by market capitalization.

Moises Ruben Kolteniuk Toyber

Director

Mr. Moises Ruben Kolteniuk Toyber serves as Director of Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. In the past, he worked in the mining sector, within the Federal Government, as well as he has been Advisor of the mining area. Additionally, he served as Member of the Board of Directors of Aeropuertos del Sureste. He holds a degree in Electromechanical Engineering from Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico and a Masters degree in Operations Research from the University of California at Berkeley.

Adriana Graciela Penaloza Alanis

Director

Ms. Adriana Graciela Penaloza Alanis serves as Director of Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. She has worked at Coordinacion Aplicada SA in the area of purchases, human resources, marketing management and international public relations. She holds a Bachelors degree in Graphics Design from Universidad Iberoamericana and a Masters degree in History of Art from Universidad Anahuac.

Luis Javier Solloa Hernandez

Independent Director

Mr. Luis Javier Solloa Hernandez serves as Independent Director of Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. He is Chairman of the Company's Audit Committee and Member of the Corporate Practices Committee. He is also Associate Partner of the firm Solloa, Tello de Meneses y Compania SC. In addition, he has been Commissioner and Member of the Board of Directors of various companies within the industrial, commercial and financial sectors. He holds a degree in Public Accounting from Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico, a diploma in Financial Engineering from Colegio de Contadores Publicos de Mexico and a diploma in High Management from Universidad Iberoamericana.

Luis Hoyo Garcia

Independent Director

Mr. Luis Hoyo Garcia serves as Independent Director of Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. He is Member of the Company's Audit Committee and Chairman of the Corporate Practices Committee. He has also been Chief Executive Officer of Agencia Aduanal Luis Hoyo and Chairman of Association of Duty Agents in Lazaro Cardenas, Michoacan. He graduated in Public Accounting from Universidad Anahuac.

Frantz Joseph Guns Devos

Independent Director

Mr. Frantz Joseph Guns Devos serves as Independent Director of Promotora y Operadora de Infraestructura, S.A.B. de C.V. He has worked at Aeropuertos del Sureste, Infraestructura Portuaria Mexicana and Ferrocarriles del Sureste. He has also been Consultant in the areas of project management, strategic planning and corporate government. He holds a Bachelors degree in Applied Economics from Universitaire Faculteiten Sint-Ignatius Antwerp (UFSIA).

In a challenging environment, with consumption slowing and rising costs, Coca-Cola Andina Bottling Company, controlled equally by the Chadwick Claro, Garcés Silva, Said Handal, and Said Somavía families, reported a profit attributable to owners of 197.164 billion pesos between January and September 2026, an increase of 17.1% compared to the same period the previous year.

The company operates in parts of Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, as well as throughout Paraguay.

In the first nine months, the consolidated sales of the bottling company reached 2.675 trillion pesos, an increase of 11.8% year-over-year, the company reported. The volume reached 691.4 million unit cases (+1.8%), while adjusted consolidated EBITDA grew by 16.9% to 488.932 billion pesos.

YOU MAY BE INTERESTED

Between July and September, the company's profit was 61.482 billion pesos, reflecting a 7.5% growth compared to the same quarter in 2025.

Consolidated net sales for the period rose by 12% to 896.609 billion pesos. According to the company, the increase was driven by higher volumes in Brazil and Chile, a rise in revenue per unit case sold, and the positive effect of currency conversion from operations in Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina.

Quarterly volume reached 226.1 million unit cases (an increase of 2.5%), and adjusted consolidated EBITDA increased by 12.1% to 149.289 billion pesos.

"These results reflect our ability to continue growing and efficiently manage costs, even in a complex environment characterized by rising oil prices," stated Miguel Ángel Peirano, the executive vice president of Coca-Cola Andina.

The executive attributed the quarterly performance to the developments in operations in Brazil, Chile, and Paraguay, along with strict cost management.

Peirano also highlighted the issuance of a green bond that the company conducted in August in the local market, amounting to 2.5 million UF, at a rate of 2.95% and maturing on September 30, 2030. The issuance achieved a spread of 65 basis points over the reference sovereign.

According to the executive, this is the lowest spread since 2019 for a AA+ corporate issuer, representing "a clear signal of market confidence in our strategy."
